lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando da Cunha | Lesson 6 -- Navigating the Unexpected

listenings.text: The thing I remember is how long it took us to work out where the problem was. On the Monday a container was held up at the port, which happens, so nobody panicked. By Wednesday two more were sitting there and customs clearance had gone from two days to nine with no explanation anybody could give us. And all that time we were looking at the port, because the port was where we could see something going wrong. The port was not the problem. The problem was an adhesive from a plant in a country I had never had a reason to think about, which had gone down three weeks earlier, and the shortage had worked its way through four other companies before it reached us. By the time we understood that, we had a backlog of about three hundred orders. What I would tell anybody is this: the place where you can see the delay is almost never the place where it started.

When we map a chain properly, the picture that comes back surprises the company almost every time, and it is not because they were careless. Each buyer sees their own suppliers, which is what they are responsible for, and each of those suppliers sees theirs. Nobody has the whole map, so nobody can see that four of your five alternatives are ultimately buying from the same plant. On paper you have five sources. In practice you have one, and you find out on the day it closes. There is a second thing that makes it worse, and it is human rather than structural. The component is cheap. It is not on anybody's list of things worth an afternoon, because attention in a purchasing department goes where the money is, and the money is in the expensive parts. So the item that can stop the whole line is precisely the item that nobody is watching. The fix is not clever. Take your bill of materials, find everything with one source, and ask what a month without it costs you. Most companies have never done it, and it takes a day.

reading.rtitle: The Part That Was Never the Risk
paras: Every company that imports keeps a list of what could go wrong, and the list is almost always about the big and visible things: the currency, the tariff, the shipping rate, the supplier who might raise the price. What the last few years taught a great many manufacturers is that chains rarely break at any of those. They break at a component nobody had thought about, made by one plant, in one country, which everybody in the industry was quietly buying from without knowing that everybody else was too.

The pattern has a name that sounds more dramatic than it is: a single point of failure. It is rarely the expensive part. It is the adhesive, the pigment, the specific chip, the one item on the bill of materials that costs almost nothing and is on the critical path of everything. And because it is cheap, nobody carries much of it, nobody has a second source for it, and nobody has run the exercise of asking what happens if it stops. When it does stop, the knock-on effect is out of all proportion to the price of the thing.

The companies that came through it best were not the ones with the best forecasts. They were the ones that had built redundancy in advance, which is an uncomfortable thing to defend to a board because it costs money every month and looks like waste in every month that nothing happens. The managers who did it describe the same conversation afterwards, in almost the same words: they had spent years being told they were carrying too much stock, and then one quarter in which nobody mentioned it again.
